exploreSites.name: Alpine Tunnel East Portal & Railroad Grade
overview: The Alpine Tunnel East Portal and approach grade are components of the larger Alpine Tunnel Historic District, a nationally significant narrow-gauge railroad engineering landscape.
The east portal, grade, Alpine Station, water facilities, Palisades, west portal, and other features are historically related but geographically distinct.

timeline.text: The Denver, South Park & Pacific excavated the 1,772-foot Alpine Tunnel beneath the Continental Divide.
The National Register district’s period of significance covers construction and operation of the high-elevation railroad corridor.
The railroad line through the tunnel was abandoned.
The east-portal landscape survives within the roughly 13-mile Alpine Tunnel Historic District corridor from Hancock to Quartz.

moreHistory: National Park Service documentation identifies the corridor’s engineering and transportation significance.
History Colorado independently preserves the district identity and its former Denver, South Park & Pacific railbed.
The east portal is interpreted as one component of the broader corridor rather than as a stand-alone history for every associated feature.

exploreSites.name: Mary Murphy Mine & Tramway
overview: The Mary Murphy was a major Chaffee County mine whose industrial system included underground workings, surface buildings, ore handling, and an aerial tramway linked to the lower terminal near Romley.
The surviving landscape shows how extraction, processing, transportation, and support structures functioned as one mining system.

timeline.text: Colorado Geological Survey records preserve contemporary assay evidence for the developing Mary Murphy property.
Mineral Survey No. 330 formally documented the property; the exact original claim-location date remains uncertain.
The mine operated nearly continuously through its principal production period.
Intermittent later activity continued after the main operating era.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey OF-01-13 documents the mine’s operating history and the Mary Murphy Gold Mining Company during its most productive years.
History Colorado records the Romley tramway terminal and the broader Chalk Creek discovery tradition.
The often-repeated 1873 date is retained only as a discovery tradition, not presented as an exact legally documented claim date.

exploreSites.name: St. Elmo Mining Town
overview: St. Elmo is one of Colorado’s best-preserved late-nineteenth-century mining towns. It grew with the Chalk Creek mining district and the railroad network serving the Alpine Tunnel corridor.
Numerous surviving buildings preserve the community landscape that supported nearby mines, transportation, commerce, and daily life.

timeline.text: The town was planned and founded under the initial name Forest City; a Post Office request led to the name St. Elmo.
Settlement expanded rapidly with mining and railroad development in the Chalk Creek district.
The Mary Murphy mine and related railroad and tramway systems remained central to the local economy.
The historic district retains an unusually intact concentration of mining-town buildings.

moreHistory: Library of Congress HABS documentation preserves the founding, renaming, town development, and mining context.
The National Register district treats St. Elmo as a community landscape rather than a single isolated structure.
Nearby mines, tram terminals, and railroad features remain distinct components even when interpreted through the town’s history.

exploreSites.name: Cleora Cemetery / Cleora Railroad-War Settlement Landscape
overview: Cleora Cemetery is a documented historic cemetery associated with the early settlement of the southern Arkansas River Valley and the Cleora community.
Its history is tied to the railroad rivalry that reshaped settlement in the valley and contributed to the rise of nearby Salida.

timeline.text: Cleora Cemetery was established during the early settlement period of the southern Arkansas River Valley.

moreHistory: The cemetery is treated as a distinct historic landscape rather than as a substitute for the broader Cleora settlement.

exploreSites.name: Crescent Moly Mine No. 100 & Mining Camp
overview: Crescent Moly Mine No. 100 and its mining camp are a documented Chaffee County resource associated with Colorado's twentieth-century molybdenum industry.
The site reflects the 1930s molybdenum boom and the wider influence of the Climax mining phenomenon on Colorado mining.

timeline.text: The Crescent Moly Mine No. 100 and mining camp developed as part of the period's molybdenum boom.

moreHistory: The mine and camp should be interpreted together while preserving individual surviving structures or workings as components of the larger site.

exploreSites.name: Garfield / Monarch Mining District
overview: The Garfield and Monarch settlements form the community core of the Monarch mining district on the east side of the Sawatch Range.
The district developed around silver-, lead-, and zinc-bearing ores and became one of southwestern Chaffee County's important hard-rock mining landscapes.

timeline.text: Ore discoveries helped launch the mining boom that produced the Garfield and Monarch settlements.
Colorado Geological Survey work documented the district's geology, mines, and two principal villages.

moreHistory: Named mines, mills, and town components remain separate records within the broader district context.

exploreSites.name: Iron City Mining Camp
overview: Iron City is a documented Chaffee County mining camp and industrial landscape with mine and mill resources recorded in federal historic-resource documentation.
The site is best understood as a mining-and-processing settlement rather than a single isolated mine feature.
moreHistory: Federal HAER documentation supports the identity of the surviving mining and milling resources; individual components should remain distinct when they can be reliably identified.

exploreSites.name: Littlejohn Mine Complex
overview: The Littlejohn Mine Complex is a documented Chaffee County mining property whose surviving buildings preserve an unusually clear picture of a small hard-rock mining operation.
Principal surviving resources include hand-hewn log buildings identified as the main cabin, burro shed or bunkhouse, and forge.

timeline.text: The Littlejohn Mine Complex was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

moreHistory: The surviving log structures and mine landscape are interpreted as one complex while keeping individual buildings identifiable as components.

exploreSites.name: Maysville Mining Community
overview: Maysville was a mining community in the Monarch-area landscape of Chaffee County and is documented in a detailed nineteenth-century panoramic view.
The surviving town and mining setting should be interpreted as a community-level record rather than as a single mine.

timeline.text: A bird's-eye view of Maysville documented the developed mining community and its built landscape.

moreHistory: The Library of Congress panoramic-map record provides a strong historic visual reference for the community.

exploreSites.name: Ohio-Colorado Smelting & Refining Co. Smokestack / Smeltertown
overview: The Ohio-Colorado Smelting & Refining Company smokestack is the dominant surviving landmark of the former Salida-area smelter and worker settlement known as Smeltertown or Kortz.
The brick-and-tile stack preserves the industrial scale of an operation that processed ore from the surrounding mining region.

timeline.text: The Ohio-Colorado smelter began operating near Salida.
The surviving smokestack was completed at a height of 365 feet.
Smelting operations at the site ended.

moreHistory: Most of the wider smelter complex disappeared, making the smokestack the clearest surviving identification feature.

exploreSites.name: Vicksburg Mining Camp
overview: Vicksburg is a historic mining camp in Chaffee County's Clear Creek Canyon and retains a recognizable concentration of mining-era town fabric.
The camp is significant as a surviving example of the communities that supported mining along the upper Clear Creek corridor.

timeline.text: Vicksburg Mining Camp was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

moreHistory: Vicksburg should remain distinct from nearby Winfield and from individual mines in the Clear Creek mining landscape.

exploreSites.name: Winfield Mining Town
overview: Winfield was a formally laid-out mining camp in Chaffee County’s Clear Creek Canyon, established to support nearby hard-rock mining.
The surviving townsite and buildings preserve the community landscape of an important late-nineteenth-century mining settlement.

timeline.text: A 120-acre townsite was laid out for the Winfield mining camp.
The National Register nomination records the camp’s heyday and an estimated population of about 1,500.
The silver-market collapse sharply reduced mining activity and settlement.
Mining activity resumed for a time after the initial decline.
The nomination records the last ore haul from the district’s operating era.
Winfield Mining Camp was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

moreHistory: The National Park Service identifies mining as Winfield’s primary area of historical significance.
NARA independently catalogs Winfield Mining Camp as National Register property 80000883.
Winfield remains distinct from nearby Vicksburg and from individual mines in the Clear Creek Canyon landscape.

exploreSites.name: Hancock Ghost Town
overview: Hancock was a mining, railroad, and logging boom town at the eastern end of the Alpine Tunnel corridor.
Its townsite and transportation remnants help explain how the Denver, South Park & Pacific supported high-country mining and tunnel operations.

timeline.text: Hancock developed as the eastern terminal community for the Alpine Tunnel railroad corridor, supporting mining, logging, and railroad activity.
Abandonment of the Alpine Tunnel line ended Hancock’s through-route role.
The town continued for a time as an end-of-line settlement before declining.
Townsite remnants and the former railroad landscape survive within the Alpine Tunnel Historic District context.

moreHistory: National Park Service documentation identifies Hancock as the district’s eastern terminus and records surviving town and railroad features.
History Colorado links Hancock to the roughly 13-mile former railroad corridor between Hancock and Quartz.
Chaffee County survey work documents depot, section-house, and water-tank facilities; exact peak population and a complete business roster remain uncertain.

exploreSites.name: Romley Mining Camp & Tram Terminal
overview: Romley was a mining camp and transportation-transfer point in the Chalk Creek district, closely tied to the Mary Murphy Mine’s aerial tramway and the railroad system serving the district.
The tram terminal, camp remains, and former railroad facilities form related but distinct parts of the Romley industrial landscape.

timeline.text: The Mary Murphy discovery began the mining history that later supported the Romley tram and transport system.
Romley developed as a mining camp and transfer point for ore and supplies moving through the Chalk Creek district.
The Mary Murphy aerial tram delivered ore into the Romley terminal system for onward railroad transport.
Mining and transportation activity declined, leaving terminal, camp, and railroad features as historic remnants.
The surviving terminal landscape is recognized and has received preservation attention.

moreHistory: Romley’s importance came from its position between a high-elevation mine and the district’s railroad network. The terminal converted aerial-tram movement into ground transportation.
Historical documentation associates Romley with a depot and turntable as well as the Mary Murphy tram terminal, showing that the site functioned as a multi-part transfer landscape.
The Romley camp and terminal should be interpreted together without treating every surviving ruin as the same structure or assigning unsupported production totals.

features.name: Mary Murphy Tramway Romley Terminal
features.note: The terminal handled ore arriving from the Mary Murphy Mine aerial tramway.

features.name: Railroad Transfer Area
features.note: Historic surveys document Romley’s depot and turntable relationship to the tram system.

features.name: Romley Mining Camp Remains
features.note: Camp remains represent the workforce and service component of the industrial site.

identificationSites.name: Banker Mine
overview: Banker Mine is a documented named mine in the Winfield area. Federal mineral and mapped-feature records support the basic identity, while conflicting commodity descriptions are reserved for further historical interpretation.

identificationSites.name: Fortune Mine
overview: Fortune Mine is a documented named mine in the Winfield quadrangle. The basic Scan record uses the supported mine identity without retaining an unverified tramway association.

identificationSites.name: Swiss Boy Mine
overview: Swiss Boy Mine is a documented Chaffee County mine with federal mineral records supporting its identity and lead-zinc and uranium-related context. Richer historical interpretation remains separate from this basic Scan record.

identificationSites.name: Tasmania Mine
overview: Tasmania Mine is a documented Winfield-area mining property associated with a proposed gravity tram and matte-smelting plans at the turn of the twentieth century. Conflicting contemporary smelter-capacity reports are preserved rather than combined into false precision.
